week_headline: Gut microbiome research takes centre stage as scientists edge closer to a stool-based early warning system for colorectal cancer

top10.claim: Comprehensive gut microbiome analysis reveals robust colorectal cancer signature
top10.verdict: There is genuinely exciting science here. Large studies — including work published in Nature Medicine and backed by the Human Microbiome Project — have found that certain gut bacteria, like Fusobacterium nucleatum and Peptostreptococcus anaerobius, appear consistently elevated in people with colorectal cancer. The word 'robust' is doing some heavy lifting though — while the signature is reproducible across several populations, it is not yet clinically validated as a standalone diagnostic tool, and diet, geography, and antibiotic history all affect your microbiome in ways that can muddy the signal.
top10.verdict_highlight: Promising signal, not a diagnostic test yet
sources: Nature Medicine — Gut microbiome and colorectal cancer studies (2019–2023)
JAMA Oncology — Fusobacterium nucleatum and CRC prognosis (2018)
Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology — microbiome-based CRC screening reviews
World Cancer Research Fund — colorectal cancer evidence report
top10.global_opinion: In the US, the FDA has not yet approved any microbiome-based colorectal cancer screening test, and colonoscopy remains the gold standard. In Europe, EFSA and national health bodies are watching this research carefully but similarly stress it is pre-clinical for screening purposes. In China and Japan, where CRC rates are rising sharply, there is strong institutional investment in gut microbiome diagnostics and a handful of pilot programmes testing stool microbiome panels alongside existing FIT tests.
top10.brit_take: The NHS is quietly interested — anything that might reduce the colonoscopy waiting list gets attention pretty quickly. But they'll want a lot more evidence before swapping a camera for a bacteria count.
